title: Foreign Policy in the American Heartland: Issues for the 120th Congress
gist: CSIS/Polity survey of 1,000 registered voters in seven battleground states (Sept 10-17, 2026) finds swing voters disapprove of tariffs (55% against) and the Iran war (56% oppose), back trade, allies and Ukraine, and favor a tough-but-calibrated China approach — with limited partisan divergence, implying electoral pressure toward engagement ahead of 2028.

themes.theme: Swing-state backlash against tariffs and Iran war

insights.claim: In a CSIS survey of 1,000 registered voters across seven battleground states, 55 percent opposed tariffs and 56 percent opposed the war with Iran.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Swing-state hostility to tariffs raises political odds that the 120th Congress and 2028 candidates push back on tariff policy — watch trade-sensitive equities and import-heavy sectors.
insights.quote: 56 percent oppose the war with Iran, and 55 percent are against tariffs

insights.claim: 62 percent of battleground-state voters said developments outside the United States affect their daily lives a great deal or a fair amount, with cost of living, rising energy costs and tariffs the most cited channels.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Voters connect foreign policy to inflation and energy prices, making energy/tariff-driven cost-of-living a key political pressure point.
insights.quote: The most frequently cited impacts related to the cost of living, including rising energy costs, and the impacts of tariffs.

insights.claim: At least 75 percent of swing-state independents, Democrats and Republicans alike believe trade with other countries is good or somewhat good for the United States.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Bipartisan pro-trade sentiment among swing voters is contrarian to the protectionist policy trend and could constrain further tariff escalation.

themes.theme: Voter support for alliances, democracy and Ukraine

insights.claim: 94 percent of battleground-state respondents said U.S. allies and partners are very or somewhat important, and 85 percent said protecting democracy and human rights worldwide is important, cutting against narratives of U.S. retrenchment.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Political base for alliance commitments is stronger than retrenchment rhetoric suggests — supportive of sustained defense spending and alliance-linked procurement.

insights.claim: 77 percent of swing-state voters consider it important to U.S. national security for Ukraine to be able to defend itself, though intensity differs: 51 percent of Democrats say very important versus 38 percent of independents and 32 percent of Republicans.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Broad but soft Republican support suggests Ukraine aid remains politically viable but vulnerable in a GOP-heavy coalition.

insights.claim: A significant majority of swing-state respondents across parties say it is important for the United States to fulfill its mutual defense commitments.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Limits political room for abandoning treaty allies; relevant for Indo-Pacific and European defense names.

insights.claim: A majority of battleground-state voters view China as both an economic and a military threat, and 11 percent believe a U.S.-China military conflict is inevitable.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Sustained hawkish public sentiment underpins continued tech controls and defense spending aimed at China.

insights.claim: A plurality of swing-state voters favor trade with China but with restrictions on sensitive technologies, which the authors read as a preference for a tough but calibrated approach.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Supports a 'small yard, high fence' style of targeted export controls rather than broad decoupling — relevant for semiconductors and dual-use tech exporters.
insights.quote: a general preference among swing-state voters for a tough but calibrated approach to managing U.S.-China relations
insights.locator: A plurality favor trade with China

themes.theme: Swing voters as driver of post-midterm foreign policy

insights.claim: The authors argue that swing-state voter preferences could determine the future direction of U.S. foreign policy and grand strategy more than any other voter group, as the 120th Congress looks toward the 2028 presidential election.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Candidates courting these states may drift toward anti-tariff, pro-alliance positions — a policy-direction signal for 2027-2028.
insights.quote: The preferences of swing-state voters in U.S. elections could determine the future direction of American foreign policy and grand strategy

insights.claim: The survey was web-based, fielded September 10-17, 2026 by Polity Research Consulting with a ±3.1 percent margin of error, and the authors say they know of no other systematic poll of foreign policy attitudes in these battleground states.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Single-poll evidence with moderate precision; treat findings as directional sentiment, not hard data.
